PROJECT 1
GOES Earth Receiver
Pull a live, full-disk image of the entire planet off a satellite parked 36,000 km up

Cost: ~$75
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) are the spacecraft behind every weather
forecast you have ever seen. They sit in geostationary orbit 35,786 km above the equator, locked to
one spot on Earth, and continuously broadcast imagery back down on an L-band downlink near 1.69
GHz. The operational satellites — GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) — transmit a signal called
HRIT that anyone can receive with a software-defined radio, a low-noise amplifier, and a dish you can
build from hardware-store parts. Because the satellite never moves relative to the ground, you aim your
antenna once and leave it — no tracking motor. The challenge is pure RF: the signal arrives near the
thermal noise floor after a 36,000 km trip, so the whole link budget hinges on a clean, low-noise front
end and enough antenna gain to close the link.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand L-band RF, low-noise amplifier and noise-figure
design, link budgets, antenna gain, and digital demodulation of a BPSK downlink. These are the
exact skills behind satellite communications, GPS, radar, and every space-to-ground link in the
industry.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 3
How It Works

• Geostationary downlink (1.69 GHz): GOES-East (GOES-19) and GOES-West (GOES-18)
broadcast HRIT near 1694.1 MHz. The signal is BPSK at roughly 400 kSym/s and carries full-disk
Earth images, regional mesoscale scans, and weather products.

• Antenna — gain is everything: After a 36,000 km path the signal is extremely weak, so you need
directional gain. A repurposed 2.4 GHz WiFi grid dish, a small offset satellite dish with a helical
feed, or a DIY cookware reflector all work. Because the bird is geostationary, you point once and
bolt it down.

• Low-noise amplifier + SAW filter: An LNA with a sub-1 dB noise figure, mounted right at the
antenna feed, sets the system sensitivity. A SAW filter near 1.69 GHz rejects cellular and WiFi that
would otherwise desensitize the receiver. This LNA-at-the-antenna placement is the single most
important decision in the build.

• Bias tee + SDR: A bias tee injects DC up the coax to power the LNA at the mast while passing RF
down to the radio. An RTL-SDR (or Airspy for more headroom) digitizes the filtered signal and
streams IQ samples to a laptop or Raspberry Pi.

• Demodulation + decode (SatDump): SatDump locks the BPSK carrier, recovers symbol timing,
applies Viterbi and Reed-Solomon forward error correction, and reassembles the packets into
full-disk and mesoscale images — the same pictures meteorologists use, pulled out of the air by
you.
Key Design Decisions
→ Why an LNA at the antenna instead of at the radio? Coax loss at 1.7 GHz is severe — several

dB per meter of cheap cable. Every dB of loss before the first amplifier adds directly to your noise
figure, so you amplify before the lossy cable degrades the signal.
→ Why geostationary instead of polar? A geostationary satellite appears fixed in the sky, so a

high-gain, narrow-beam dish can be aimed once and left. A polar satellite races across the sky and
would demand a motorized tracker — which is exactly Project 3's problem.
→ Why BPSK for the downlink? BPSK is the most power-efficient digital modulation — it tolerates

the lowest signal-to-noise ratio of any common scheme. When you are link-budget starved from
36,000 km, you trade data rate for the robustness that lets the link close at all.

Build Steps

Build or repurpose the antenna: Start with a 2.4 GHz WiFi grid dish or a small offset satellite dish.
Add a feed tuned for 1.69 GHz — a 3–5 turn helical feed wound from copper wire over a ground plane
works well and is circularly polarized, matching the satellite. Mount it on a rigid tripod.

Mount the LNA at the feed: Connect the LNA + SAW filter directly to the antenna feed with the
shortest possible pigtail — ideally screwed straight onto the connector. This is non-negotiable: amplify
before the coax. Weatherproof the joint if it lives outside.

Power it through the bias tee: Insert the bias tee inline at the radio end, feed it 5 V, and verify the
LNA draws current. Confirm RF passes to the SDR. A common failure is a bias-tee voltage or polarity
mismatch that never powers the LNA — check it with a multimeter.

Aim the dish (once): Look up the azimuth and elevation for GOES-East or GOES-West from your
location with any satellite-finder app. Geostationary means a single fixed bearing. Peak the signal in
SatDump by nudging the dish a degree at a time until the BPSK shoulders rise out of the noise.

Decode in SatDump: Select the GOES HRIT pipeline, set the sample rate, and start. Once locked you
will see the constellation snap to two BPSK points and packets flow. Let a full-disk scan complete and
watch a live image of the entire planet assemble on your screen. Save the GeoTIFF and post the
timestamp.

PROJECT 2
Meteor-M2 Weather Receiver

Image your own city from a satellite screaming overhead at 137 MHz, decoded line by
line

Cost: ~$40
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

For years, the way most people received their first satellite image was the NOAA APT signal on 137
MHz — but in 2025 the last NOAA APT satellite was decommissioned and that signal went silent for
good. The torch has passed to the Russian Meteor-M series, whose M2-3 and M2-4 satellites transmit
a sharper, digital signal called LRPT in the same easy-to-reach 137 MHz band. Unlike geostationary
GOES, these are polar-orbiting satellites in low Earth orbit, sweeping over your location a few times a
day and painting a strip of the planet beneath them. The whole receive chain costs about the price of a
textbook: an RTL-SDR, a simple antenna you can build from two pieces of wire, and free software. It is
the most accessible image-from-space project that still actually works in 2026.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand VHF reception, antenna design and polarization
(why satellites use circular polarization), Doppler shift, and digital QPSK demodulation with forward
error correction — the same RF fundamentals that scale all the way up to GOES and deep-space
communication.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 7
How It Works

• Polar LRPT downlink (137 MHz): Meteor-M2-3 and M2-4 transmit LRPT near 137.9 MHz (137.1
MHz backup). Unlike the old analog NOAA APT, LRPT is digital QPSK at about 72 kbps, carrying a
crisper multi-spectral image.

• A satellite that moves: These satellites orbit roughly 800 km up in a sun-synchronous polar orbit,
crossing your sky in about 12–15 minutes per pass. You capture a strip of Earth directly under the
ground track — typically your region and a few hundred km either side.

• Antenna and polarization: A V-dipole (two ~50 cm wires at about 120 degrees) is the simplest
antenna; a QFH (quadrifilar helix) is omnidirectional and better for the ever-changing pass
geometry. Satellites transmit circular polarization, which is why a QFH outperforms a flat dipole on
low passes.

• Optional LNA for the city: In a quiet rural spot the SDR alone can decode a high pass. In a city full
of RF noise, a 137 MHz SAW-filtered LNA at the antenna dramatically improves results by rejecting
pagers, FM broadcast, and other interference.

• Doppler and decode (SatDump): Because the satellite is moving fast, its frequency shifts by several
kHz across the pass (Doppler). SatDump tracks the satellite by its orbital elements, corrects
Doppler, demodulates the QPSK, applies error correction, and assembles the decoded image.

Build Steps

Build the V-dipole: Cut two wires about 50 cm each (quarter-wave at 137 MHz). Mount them at
roughly 120 degrees in a horizontal V pointing up. Connect to coax: one leg to center, one to shield.
Drop the coax straight down behind the antenna so it acts as a decoupling stub.

Add the LNA if needed: For urban environments, place the 137 MHz SAW LNA at the antenna and
power it via the bias tee. Verify the LNA is the filtered 1581 VHF version — an ADS-B LNA at the wrong
frequency will hurt, not help.

Predict a pass: Use a tracker (Look4Sat on Android, or SatDump's built-in tracker) to find the next
Meteor-M2-3 or M2-4 pass above about 20 degrees elevation. Note AOS (acquisition of signal) and
LOS times. Higher passes give far better images.

Record the pass: In SatDump, select the Meteor M2-x LRPT pipeline (72k mode; try 80k if a newly
commissioned bird will not sync). Set gain manually to about 30 dB — do NOT use AGC, which
corrupts the narrow LRPT signal. Start a minute before AOS.

Decode and overlay: After the pass, SatDump demodulates and decodes the image. Add map
overlays — shorelines and city markers — to prove it is your own region. Compare consecutive passes
to watch weather systems move across your area.
Interview Questions:
→ Why did NOAA APT reception stop working, and what replaced it?
→ Why do weather satellites transmit circular polarization, and how does that affect antenna choice?
→ What causes the Doppler shift across a pass, and how is it corrected?
→ What is the advantage of digital LRPT (QPSK) over the old analog APT?
→ Why must you disable AGC on the SDR for narrowband satellite signals?
→ How does a quadrifilar helix achieve an omnidirectional, circularly-polarized pattern?

PROJECT 3
Reaction-Wheel Attitude Controller

A spinning flywheel rotates and holds a platform's heading — how satellites point
without thrusters

Cost: ~$50
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

A satellite in orbit has no ground to push against, so how does it turn to point a camera or antenna?
Most spacecraft use reaction wheels: spin a flywheel one way and conservation of angular momentum
rotates the spacecraft the other way. Speed the wheel up or slow it down and you apply precise torque
to the body — no fuel, no thrusters. This project builds a single-axis reaction-wheel platform (or the
dramatic reaction-wheel pendulum that balances on an edge): an IMU senses the platform's angle, a
control loop computes the torque needed, and a motor accelerates a flywheel to deliver it. It is the
cleanest possible demonstration of real attitude control — the same principle flying on every imaging
satellite, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the control gyros of the ISS.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand closed-loop control (PID/LQR), sensor fusion,
BLDC motor torque control, and real-time embedded firmware. Attitude determination and control is
a core aerospace discipline, and the same fundamentals underpin robotics, drones, and
self-balancing vehicles.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 10
How It Works

• Conservation of angular momentum: The platform sits on a low-friction bearing. When the motor
accelerates the flywheel clockwise, the platform reacts by rotating counter-clockwise. The torque on
the body equals the rate of change of the wheel's angular momentum — so wheel acceleration is
your control input.

• IMU attitude sensing: An MPU-6050 or BNO055 IMU fuses its gyroscope and accelerometer to
estimate the platform's tilt angle and angular rate. A complementary or Kalman filter blends the
drift-free-but-noisy accelerometer with the smooth-but-drifting gyro.

• The control loop: A PID (or LQR) controller takes the angle error and computes a commanded
wheel torque. For the balancing-pendulum version it must stabilize an inherently unstable
equilibrium — like balancing a broom on your palm, but a thousand times a second.

• BLDC torque control: A brushless gimbal motor spins the flywheel. A field-oriented control (FOC)
driver regulates motor current, and since torque is proportional to current, this gives direct, smooth
torque control — far better than crude PWM speed control.

• Momentum saturation: If the platform keeps disturbing in one direction, the wheel spins faster and
faster until it hits its limit — saturation. Real satellites dump this momentum with magnetorquers or
thrusters. On the bench you will watch the wheel max out and learn why momentum management
matters.

Build Steps

Build the mechanics: Mount the BLDC motor on a rigid arm or platform that pivots on a single
low-friction bearing. Attach a balanced flywheel to the shaft — mass at the rim maximizes moment of
inertia per gram. Balance it so it does not introduce its own torque.

Wire motor + driver: Connect the three BLDC phases to the FOC driver and the driver to the MCU.
Power from the LiPo with appropriate current limits. Run the FOC library's alignment routine so the
controller learns the rotor's electrical zero.

Bring up the IMU: Mount the IMU rigidly on the platform, not on the vibrating motor. Read gyro and
accelerometer over I2C at about 1 kHz. Implement a complementary filter for a clean tilt-angle
estimate. Verify the angle tracks reality as you tilt the platform by hand.

Close the loop: Implement PID: error = target angle minus measured angle; output = commanded
motor current (torque). Start with proportional gain only, add derivative for damping, then a little
integral. Tune until the platform holds its target heading and rejects a finger-push disturbance.

Demonstrate and characterize: Command a step change in heading and film the platform snapping
to the new angle. For the pendulum build, show it balancing upright on its edge. Log angle vs. time to
show your step response — overshoot, settling time, steady-state error — the language of control
engineering.
Interview Questions:
→ How does conservation of angular momentum let a reaction wheel rotate a spacecraft?
→ Why is motor current (torque) control better than PWM speed control here?
→ What is reaction-wheel saturation, and how do real satellites desaturate?
→ How does a complementary or Kalman filter fuse gyro and accelerometer data?
→ Why is the balancing pendulum unstable, and what does that demand of the controller?
→ How would you extend single-axis control to full 3-axis attitude control?

PROJECT 4
Camera Star Tracker

Point it at the night sky — it identifies the stars and outputs your exact 3-axis
orientation

Cost: ~$60
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

Before a satellite can point at anything, it has to know which way it is already facing — and the most
accurate way to do that in space is to look at the stars. A star tracker photographs a patch of sky,
identifies the star pattern by matching it against an onboard catalog, and from that computes the
spacecraft's precise 3-axis orientation, accurate to arc-seconds. This is the highest-precision attitude
sensor ever flown, and you can build a working one: a camera with a fast lens, a small computer, and
an open-source lost-in-space plate-solving algorithm that figures out where you are pointed with zero
prior information. Pair it with Project 3's reaction wheel and you have both halves of a real spacecraft's
attitude system — sensing and actuation.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand low-light image sensors and optics (f-number,
exposure), embedded computer vision, star-identification algorithms, and the coordinate-frame math
(quaternions) behind pointing systems. Star trackers are flagship aerospace GNC hardware —
building one signals you can work on real spacecraft guidance.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 13
How It Works

• Fast lens + low-light sensor: Stars are dim, so the optics matter most. A fast lens (f/1.4–f/2) gathers
maximum light; a sensitive CMOS sensor (a Raspberry Pi HQ camera or a Sony IMX module) with a
multi-second exposure captures enough stars per frame to identify a pattern. Monochrome and
longer exposure both help.

• Star centroiding: The software thresholds the image to separate stars from background, then
computes the sub-pixel centroid of each star blob. Centroiding to a fraction of a pixel is what gives
the tracker its arc-second accuracy — far finer than the pixel grid itself.

• Pattern matching (lost in space): The key trick: the angular distances between stars form a unique
fingerprint. An open-source solver like Tetra3 hashes these geometric patterns and matches them
against a precomputed catalog — identifying exactly which stars you are looking at with no prior
orientation estimate.

• Attitude solve: Once stars are identified, their known catalog positions (right ascension and
declination) plus their measured pixel positions let the solver compute the rotation that maps one to
the other. The result is the camera's orientation, expressed as a quaternion or rotation matrix.

• Edge compute: All of this runs on a Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W or Pi 4). The solve takes well under a
second per frame — fast enough to output a continuous attitude estimate, exactly as a real star
tracker feeds a spacecraft's control system.

Build Steps

Assemble the optics: Fit the fast C-mount lens to the camera via the adapter. Focus at infinity on a
distant light at night — the sharpest star points give the best centroids. A rigid, vibration-free mount is
essential; any blur smears stars and kills accuracy.

Set up the compute: Flash the Pi and install Python, OpenCV, and the Tetra3 star-identification
library. Download or generate the star-catalog database tuned to your lens's field of view (Tetra3 builds
this from a catalog such as Hipparcos).

Capture night-sky frames: Take test exposures of a few seconds pointed at a clear sky. Tune
exposure and gain until you reliably capture a dozen-plus stars per frame without saturating the
brightest ones. Confirm stars appear as crisp points, not streaks.

Run the solver: Feed a frame to Tetra3. It centroids the stars, matches the pattern, and returns the
celestial coordinates the camera is pointed at, plus a roll angle. Verify against a planetarium app
(Stellarium) aimed at the same patch of sky.

Output continuous attitude: Loop the capture-and-solve at a steady cadence, printing the live
quaternion. Mount the tracker on Project 3's reaction-wheel platform and you have closed the full loop:
the star tracker says where you point, the wheel turns you where you want.

→ How does sub-pixel centroiding achieve accuracy finer than the pixel pitch?

PROJECT 5
GPS-Disciplined Oscillator

Lock a local oscillator to the atomic clocks aboard GPS satellites for parts-per-billion
accuracy

Cost: ~$30
Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters

Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock, and the timing signal it broadcasts is disciplined to within
nanoseconds of the global time standard. A GPS-disciplined oscillator borrows that accuracy: it takes
the once-per-second pulse (1PPS) from a cheap GPS receiver and uses it to steer a local crystal
oscillator so its frequency is locked, long-term, to atomic precision — parts-per-billion or better. This is
the quiet workhorse of every serious RF lab, cellular base station, and test bench: the reference that
everything else is measured against. Building one teaches you precision timing, control loops, and the
discipline of measuring frequency accurately — and it is the most affordable project in this guide.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand precision frequency references, phase-locked
control loops, GNSS timing (1PPS), oscillator steering via DAC or varactor, and how to characterize
stability with Allan deviation. Timing and synchronization is foundational to communications, radar,
and instrumentation — and surprisingly few engineers actually understand it.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 16
How It Works

• The 1PPS reference: A GPS receiver outputs a one-pulse-per-second signal whose rising edge is
aligned to GPS system time — itself steered by the atomic clocks aboard the satellites. The edge is
accurate to tens of nanoseconds, but it jitters pulse-to-pulse, so it is a great long-term reference and
a poor short-term one.

• The local oscillator: An OCXO (oven-controlled crystal oscillator) is extremely stable
second-to-second but slowly drifts over hours and temperature. It is the opposite of GPS: great
short-term, poor long-term. The whole idea is to combine the two.

• Phase comparison: The MCU divides the OCXO (e.g. 10 MHz) down to 1 Hz and measures the time
error between that and the GPS 1PPS using a hardware timer's input capture. This error, in
nanoseconds, is the signal the control loop drives to zero.

• The loop filter: A slow software control loop — a long time constant of many seconds to minutes —
averages out the GPS jitter and computes a correction. Too fast and you chase GPS noise; too
slow and you fail to track drift. This tradeoff is the heart of the design.

• Steering the oscillator: The correction drives a DAC that sets the OCXO's electronic frequency
control (EFC) voltage, nudging it a few parts-per-billion. Over minutes the loop converges and the
OCXO is disciplined — its frequency now traceable to the same standard as the satellites overhead.

Build Steps

Get a GPS fix + 1PPS: Wire the GPS module and antenna; confirm it acquires satellites and outputs a
clean 1PPS. Scope the pulse — it should be rock-steady at 1 Hz once locked. Place the antenna with a
clear sky view.

Run the OCXO free: Power the OCXO and let its oven stabilize for a few minutes. Feed its 10 MHz
into an MCU timer and measure its frequency against the 1PPS, uncorrected, first. You will see it is off
by a small, slowly changing amount — that drift is what you will cancel.

Measure phase error: Use the MCU's input-capture timer to timestamp both the divided OCXO edge
and the GPS 1PPS edge. The difference is your phase error in nanoseconds. Stream it to the OLED
and watch it wander as the OCXO drifts.

Close the discipline loop: Implement a slow PI control loop: integrate the averaged phase error and
output a DAC value to the OCXO's EFC pin. Choose a long time constant (tens of seconds) so GPS
jitter is averaged out. Watch the error converge toward zero and stay there.

Characterize stability: Log the phase error over hours and compute the Allan deviation — the
standard measure of oscillator stability. Show the disciplined OCXO beats both the free-running OCXO
(long-term) and raw GPS (short-term). That crossover plot is the money shot.
Interview Questions:
→ Why combine a GPS receiver and an OCXO — what does each contribute?
→ Why is the 1PPS a good long-term reference but a poor short-term one?
→ How do you measure the phase error between the oscillator and the 1PPS?
→ How does the loop time constant trade jitter rejection against drift tracking?
→ What is Allan deviation and why is it the right metric for oscillator stability?
→ What is holdover, and how should the loop behave when GPS signal is lost?

PROJECT 6
Cosmic-Ray Muon Detector

Every flash is a particle born from a cosmic ray hitting the atmosphere, passing
through your desk

Cost: ~$75
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

Right now, particles created when cosmic rays from exploding stars and distant galaxies slam into the
upper atmosphere are raining down through your body — about one muon through every square
centimeter every minute. You can build an instrument that catches them. When a muon passes through
a plastic scintillator it leaves a tiny flash of light; a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) turns that flash into an
electrical pulse, a fast amplifier boosts it, and a discriminator counts it. This is real particle-physics
instrumentation — the same detection principle used at CERN — built on your bench for under $80. It
is also the deepest analog challenge in this guide: catching a microsecond flash of a few hundred
photons demands genuinely low-noise, high-speed front-end design.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand SiPM biasing and temperature compensation,
low-noise transimpedance amplification, fast pulse discrimination, and coincidence detection. This is
high-speed, low-noise analog at the edge of what is possible — exactly the skill set behind medical
imaging, LIDAR, and scientific instrumentation.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 19
How It Works

• The scintillator: A block of plastic scintillator (cast PVT, or a surplus offcut) emits a brief flash of blue
light when a charged particle deposits energy crossing it. A single muon produces only a few
hundred to a few thousand photons — faint and fast, lasting nanoseconds.

• Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM): A SiPM is an array of avalanche photodiodes biased just above
breakdown, giving enormous gain (around 106) — enough to turn a handful of photons into a
measurable current pulse. It replaces the bulky, high-voltage photomultiplier tubes of old with a 6
mm chip running on about 29 V.

• Precise bias + temperature: A SiPM's gain is steeply sensitive to bias voltage and temperature, so a
stable, low-noise bias supply (a quiet boost converter plus filtering) is critical. Drift the voltage and
your count rate drifts with it — which is why real systems add temperature compensation.

• Fast amplifier: A transimpedance or voltage amplifier with enough bandwidth (tens of MHz) converts
the SiPM's fast current spike into a clean voltage pulse without smearing it. Layout matters here —
short traces, good grounding, and supply bypassing keep noise below the tiny signal.

• Discrimination and counting: A comparator fires when a pulse exceeds a threshold set just above
the noise floor, producing a clean digital tick per event. An MCU counts ticks and shows the muon
rate on an OLED. Add a second detector and require coincidence — only count when both fire at
once — to reject electrical noise and confirm real through-going particles.

Build Steps

Couple SiPM to scintillator: Wrap the scintillator in reflective foil (Tyvek or aluminized mylar), leaving
one face for the SiPM. Optically couple the SiPM to that face with optical grease or a clear pad. Seal
everything in a light-tight enclosure — ambient light will swamp the SiPM instantly.

Build the bias supply: Use an adjustable boost converter for the SiPM bias (about 29 V; check your
SiPM's breakdown plus overvoltage spec). Filter it heavily with RC stages — any ripple shows up as
noise. Set the exact voltage with a multimeter before connecting the SiPM.

Amplify the pulse: Build the fast amplifier on a compact board with a ground plane. Keep the
SiPM-to-amp path short. Scope the output: cosmic muons appear as occasional fast spikes a few times
a second above the noise.

Set the discriminator: Feed the amplified signal to the comparator. Set the threshold just above the
noise floor — high enough to ignore noise, low enough to catch real pulses. Each crossing generates
one clean digital pulse to the MCU.

Count and (optionally) coincidence: Program the MCU to count pulses and show the muon rate on
the OLED. Expect very roughly one count per cm2 per minute of detector area. For a rigorous version,
build a second detector and only count simultaneous hits — coincidence proves you are seeing real
particles, not noise.
Interview Questions:
→ How does a scintillator plus SiPM convert a passing particle into an electrical pulse?
→ Why is a SiPM's bias voltage so critical, and how does temperature affect its gain?
→ What bandwidth does the amplifier need, and why does layout matter for low-noise design?
→ How do you set the discriminator threshold relative to the noise floor?
→ Why does coincidence detection between two scintillators reject false counts?
→ Roughly what muon flux do you expect at sea level, and how would you measure efficiency?

Now it fits on your bench.

Satellite downlinks. Attitude control. Precision timing. Particle detection. These are not toy demos —
they are the actual subsystems of spacecraft and the instruments of space science, rebuilt with a
software-defined radio, a microcontroller, and parts that cost less than a textbook. The hard parts are
real: closing a link budget from 36,000 km, stabilizing an unstable control loop a thousand times a
second, catching a nanosecond flash of a few hundred photons. That difficulty is the point.

Aerospace, defense, and the new commercial-space boom are hiring engineers who can actually build
this hardware — not just describe it. A working demo of any one of these puts you in a different
conversation.

Build even one of these. Log the link budget, screenshot the decoded image, plot the step response
or the Allan deviation. Put it on your GitHub with a proper README. You will have a portfolio piece
that makes an aerospace interviewer lean forward.
